pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-mee-dah' — three even syllables, with the middle vowel bright and short.

kin.label: Japanese
kin.form: 阿弥陀 (Amida), the Japanese reading of the Sanskrit name Amitābha

pronunciation.note: Amida is Tier 2: the Japanese form loses the long ā and aspirated bh of the Sanskrit, so it preserves nothing ASCII cannot already write. The name's power is devotional, not orthographic.

domains.title: Buddha of Immeasurable Light
domains.subtitle: Pure Land, Faith, and the Promise of Rebirth
domains.lead: Amida is the Japanese face of Amitābha, the Buddha whose boundless light and life created a pure land in the west. For more than a thousand years, his name has been the refuge of millions: Namu Amida Butsu, 'I take refuge in Amida Buddha.' The promise is radical — even ordinary people, burdened by karma they cannot escape, can be reborn in his Pure Land and attain enlightenment.

cards.name: Immeasurable Light
cards.desc: His name means light without limit, dispelling the darkness of ignorance and karma.

cards.name: Pure Land (Sukhāvatī)
cards.desc: The western paradise where rebirth guarantees progress toward buddhahood.

cards.name: Name as Vow
cards.desc: Honen and Shinran taught that calling his name with faith is itself the path.

cards.name: Welcoming Descent
cards.desc: Raigō art shows Amida descending with bodhisattvas to meet the dying.

symbols.name: Lotus seat
symbols.meaning: Purity and transcendence, the throne from which he teaches

symbols.name: Mudrā of welcome
symbols.meaning: The hand gesture in raigō images, beckoning the faithful to the Pure Land

symbols.name: Beaded rosary
symbols.meaning: The nenbutsu recited bead by bead: Namu Amida Butsu

mythology.lead: Amida's mythology is rooted in Indian Mahāyāna texts, transmitted through China, and transformed in Japan into one of the most influential forms of Buddhist devotion.

myths.title: The Vows of Dharmākara
myths.text: Long ago, the monk Dharmākara made forty-eight vows before a former Buddha. The eighteenth vow became the foundation of Pure Land faith: beings who sincerely desired rebirth in his Pure Land and called his name would be welcomed there. After countless ages of practice, Dharmākara fulfilled these vows and became Amida Buddha, presiding over Sukhāvatī, the Land of Bliss.

myths.title: Honen and the Single Practice
myths.text: In the 12th century, the monk Hōnen declared that in the degenerate age of the Dharma, ordinary people could not achieve enlightenment by their own effort. The single practice of calling Amida's name — nenbutsu — was sufficient. His disciple Shinran deepened this into a path of absolute reliance on Amida's Other Power (tariki), shaping Jōdo Shinshū, the largest Buddhist denomination in Japan.

myths.title: The Welcoming Descent
myths.text: Raigō paintings show Amida descending on clouds, attended by the bodhisattvas Kannon and Seishi, to meet the dying at the moment of death. These images became a central focus of deathbed practice and mortuary culture, transforming the fear of death into a vision of welcome.

lore.syncretism: Amida is inseparable from the broader Amitābha cult across East Asia. In China he is Ēmítuó; in Korea, Amit'a; in Tibet, Öpakmé. Japanese Pure Land Buddhism, however, made the nenbutsu into a mass movement, and Amida became a household name. His imagery also merged with native kami cults: some local deities were identified as manifestations of Amida, and the dying were encouraged to face west, toward both the setting sun and the Pure Land.
lore.culturalLegacy: Amida's name is among the most recited in Japanese religious history. Temples such as Hōryūji, Byōdōin, and Zenkōji preserve colossal Amida images. The phrase Namu Amida Butsu appears in literature, film, and everyday speech as an expression of gratitude or resignation. Byōdōin's Phoenix Hall, depicted on the 10-yen coin, is an architectural hymn to the Pure Land.
lore.extendedMeditation: Amida asks what it means to be saved by grace rather than effort. The Pure Land teaching does not deny discipline; it relocates the power. The name itself becomes the practice, and faith becomes the opening through which boundless light enters.
lore.archaeology: Byōdōin at Uji (1053 CE) is the most famous Amida temple in Japan, built as a Pure Land paradise hall and now a UNESCO site. Its Amida image by Jōchō set the standard for Heian-period Buddhist sculpture. Zenkōji in Nagano has housed a hidden Amida triad since the 7th century, attracting pilgrims from across the archipelago.
